The first thing Mara found in the wall was a teaspoon.

It lay in the dust beneath the plaster, its handle bent into the shape of a question mark. She assumed a builder had dropped it there years ago, until she found the marble, the red mitten, and an envelope addressed in her mother’s handwriting to someone named *Tomorrow*.

Mara sat back on her heels.

She had come to the house to make it ready for sale. Her mother had been dead for three months, and the rooms still seemed organized around the expectation of her return: a cardigan on the kitchen chair, a grocery list held to the refrigerator with a magnet shaped like a pear. Mara had made steady progress through the cupboards, but the loose plaster in the hallway had turned an afternoon’s work into something else.

She opened the envelope.

Inside was a slip of paper.

*Ask Mara about the bird.*

That was all. No date, no explanation. Mara turned it over, hoping for more, but the back was blank.

She took the paper into the kitchen and looked at it while the kettle boiled. Her mother had always left herself notes: *Call dentist*, *Beans soaking*, *Don’t forget Jan’s birthday again*. Yet Mara could not remember her ever asking about a bird.

She called her brother.

“Did Mum ever tell you about something she put in the hallway wall?”

“Was it money?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

“There’s a note in there about a bird.”

He was quiet for a moment. “You had a bird.”

“I did?”

“Not properly. It flew into the kitchen window. You made a box for it.”

Mara looked out at the kitchen window. The glass had been replaced years ago; she remembered that much.

“What happened to it?”

“I don’t know. You wouldn’t let me near it.”

After the call, she carried her tea back to the hallway. She crouched beside the opening and reached inside. Her fingers found a smooth wooden button, a pencil worn down to a stub, and a photograph of her and her brother standing in the garden. They were children in the picture. Mara held a shoebox against her chest, and both of them looked fiercely at the camera.

The box had holes punched in its lid.

That evening she called her brother again.

“I found a photograph. You were there.”

“I told you I was there.”

“You said I wouldn’t let you near it.”

“I think that’s why I remember.”

Together they pieced it out. The bird had been a thrush, or perhaps a starling. Mara had lined the box with one of their father’s socks. Their mother had telephoned a wildlife rescue, then driven them all there with the box on Mara’s lap.

“And?” Mara said.

“And what?”

“Did the bird live?”

“I don’t know.”

Mara almost said that surely their mother would have known, but she could picture her now, standing at the kitchen counter and writing the note. She must have meant to ask the next time they spoke. Perhaps Mara had mentioned the bird in passing, years after it happened, and her mother had wanted to hear the rest of the story.

Mara looked again at the photograph. Her brother’s arm was reaching across behind her, his hand resting on the bottom of the box. She had not noticed it at first.

“I think you helped me carry it,” she said.

“Of course I did.”

She put the photograph and the note on the mantelpiece. The other things went into a tin for her brother to look through when he came on Saturday. He might remember the red mitten, too, or know why anyone had bent a perfectly good spoon.
